title: Google Business Profile in 2026: a practical local SEO playbook
metaTitle: Google Business Profile: A 2026 Local SEO Playbook
metaDescription: Get more from your Google Business Profile in 2026: categories, review rules, photos, posts, life after Q&A, NAP consistency and service-area settings.
lead: For a clinic, café or plumber, the Business Profile is often the first and only thing a customer sees before calling. Google says local results depend mainly on relevance, distance and prominence, and that there is no way to pay for a better local ranking. This playbook covers the settings and habits you control, and the review rules that can get a profile restricted.
keyPoints: Pick the fewest, most specific categories that complete “this business is a…”, and use your business name exactly as it appears on your signage.
Ask every customer for a review, never reward them for it and never filter for happy customers; Google can block new reviews and show a public warning on profiles that break its rules.
Service-area businesses should hide a home address and keep their area within about two hours' drive of their base.
The public Q&A section has largely gone, so answer common questions in your profile details, review replies and website.
Your name, address and phone number should match everywhere, from your website to Justdial and IndiaMART.

sections.heading: How Google decides local rankings
paragraphs: Google's own help page names three factors. Relevance is how well a profile matches the search; distance is how far the business is from the searcher or the place named in the query; prominence is how well known the business is, informed by things like links and reviews. Google states that more reviews and positive ratings can help, and that a better ranking can't be requested or bought.
Distance is the one factor you can't change, so the work goes into relevance, through accurate categories, services and descriptions, and prominence, through reviews, mentions and a strong website.

sections.heading: Name, categories and attributes
paragraphs: Your profile name must match the real-world name on your signage and stationery. Adding keywords, locations or taglines, as in “Sharma Dental Clinic – Best Dentist in Lajpat Nagar”, breaks Google's guidelines and invites suspension or edits by other users. Then work through the rest of the profile:
bullets: Choose a primary category that describes what the business is, not what it has.
Add secondary categories only for genuinely separate core services.
Fill in services and products with plain descriptions that use the words customers use.
Set the attributes that apply, such as wheelchair access, online appointments or languages spoken.
Write the business description for people: what you do, for whom and where, without stuffing it with city names.

sections.heading: Address, service areas and virtual offices
paragraphs: The address must be the precise location where you serve customers, with one profile per location. P.O. boxes and remote mailboxes aren't allowed, and a virtual office qualifies only if it is staffed during business hours.

If you travel to customers, as a pest-control business in Noida or a home tutor in Kochi does, set a service area and hide your address. Google's guidelines say the area shouldn't extend much beyond about two hours' driving time from your base. Businesses that receive customers at a staffed location and also travel can show the address and a service area together. Our [home services page](/industries/home-services) covers the wider marketing picture for businesses that work on-site.

sections.heading: Review rules Google enforces
paragraphs: Google's Maps review policies are stricter than many owners realize. Under its fake-engagement rules, a business must not:
bullets: Offer money, discounts, free services or other incentives for reviews, or for changing or removing them.
Ask only happy customers for reviews, a practice often called review gating.
Discourage or prevent negative reviews.
Set staff quotas for reviews or pressure customers to write one while on the premises.
Post reviews from owners, employees or anyone else with a conflict of interest.

sections.heading: What happens when the rules are broken
paragraphs: Google deletes reviews that break these rules, and it can go further: stopping a profile from receiving new reviews for a period, unpublishing its existing reviews and showing customers a warning that fake reviews were removed. Owners are emailed before a restriction applies and can appeal.

Indian law points the same way. Paid or fabricated reviews can amount to misleading advertising or an unfair trade practice under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, and the government's 2022 framework built on the standard IS 19000:2022 sets out how reviews should be collected, moderated and published. Our [reputation management](/reputation-management) service builds review programs that stay inside these lines.

sections.heading: Asking for reviews and replying well
paragraphs: A consistent, neutral request process earns more reviews than occasional pushes, and well-written replies are read by every future visitor. A routine that stays within the rules:
bullets: Ask everyone at the same point in the journey, for example with a WhatsApp message containing your review link after each completed job.
Keep the request neutral, such as “we'd value your honest feedback”, rather than asking for five stars.
Reply to every review within a few days, mentioning something specific in positive ones.
For negative reviews, acknowledge the issue, avoid arguing in public and offer a direct contact to resolve it.
Clinics and other confidential services should never confirm that a reviewer was a patient or client, or mention any treatment.
Report reviews that break Google's policies through your profile, but expect only clear violations to come down.

sections.heading: Photos, videos, posts and hours
paragraphs: Google's own tips include adding photos and videos and keeping hours, including special hours, accurate. Real images beat stock ones: the shopfront as seen from the street so people recognize it, the interior, your team at work and examples of finished jobs. Beyond that:
bullets: Update holiday and festival hours ahead of Diwali, Eid, Christmas or local closures.
Use posts for offers, events, new services and seasonal reminders, each with a clear call to action.
Add short videos of the space or the work, especially for salons, gyms and restaurants.
Check photos that customers upload, and report anything inappropriate or misleading.

sections.heading: Life after Q&A
paragraphs: Google shut down its Business Profile Q&A API in November 2025, and the public questions-and-answers section has since disappeared from most profiles. In the Google Maps app in some markets, listings now offer AI-generated answers to visitors' questions, drawn from profile information, reviews and the business's website.

That makes your own information the raw material for those answers. Keep attributes, services, hours and descriptions complete, publish a clear FAQ on your website, and treat review replies as public answers, because a reply explaining your parking or appointment policy is read by everyone who comes later.

sections.heading: Keep NAP details consistent
paragraphs: NAP stands for name, address and phone number. When these differ across your website, Business Profile and directories, Google and AI assistants alike have to guess which version is right. To keep them aligned:
bullets: List every place your business appears: website, Google, Bing Places, Apple Business Connect, Justdial, IndiaMART, Practo or Zomato where relevant, and social profiles.
Correct old phone numbers and previous addresses, especially after a move.
Use one English spelling of your name, and settle on one Hindi or regional spelling if you use one.
Add LocalBusiness structured data to your website that matches the profile exactly.

sections.heading: A monthly routine that keeps a profile healthy
paragraphs: Local visibility is one part of a wider [SEO](/seo) program. If you'd like a profile audit and review plan, [book a free consultation](/book-consultation). Otherwise, block out an hour each month to:
bullets: Review edits that Google or users have suggested, and correct anything wrong.
Reply to every new review and note recurring complaints for the team.
Add a few new photos and at least one post.
Check hours for upcoming holidays.
Look at profile performance: calls, direction requests and website clicks.

faqs.q: Can I offer a discount in exchange for a Google review?
faqs.a: No. Google's policies prohibit incentives for reviews, including discounts and freebies, whether or not you ask for a positive rating. You can ask every customer for honest feedback as long as no reward is attached.

faqs.q: Should a home-based business show its address?
faqs.a: Not if customers don't visit you. Service-area businesses should hide the address and set the areas they serve instead, showing an address only if customers are received there during stated hours.

faqs.q: How many categories should I choose?
faqs.a: As few as accurately describe your core business. Pick the most specific primary category available and add secondary ones only for distinct core services, never as keywords or to describe amenities.

faqs.q: Can I get a negative review removed?
faqs.a: Only if it breaks Google's content policies, for example spam, a conflict of interest or offensive content. Report it from your profile; for genuine criticism, a calm and specific reply usually does more for your reputation than removal would.
